newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH COALITION STILL SPLIT ON TAXES - CIMOSZEWICZ.
newsitem.headline: POLISH COALITION STILL SPLIT ON TAXES - CIMOSZEWICZ.

text.p: Poland's ruling coalition remains divided on taxes ahead of Wednesday's Senate debate on income tax bills, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said on Tuesday.

"I have to say, with regret, that so far the coalition parties have failed to agree a common stand on taxes, therefore the government will present its own proposals (to the Senate)," Cimoszewicz told a news briefing.

The Senate is due to vote this week on the lower house's tax bill, which introduces deep cuts in taxes for the lowest paid and which the government opposes as economically unrealistic, proposing instead a more moderate tax-cut plan.
"I believe that there will be a (Senate) majority ready to pass such bills which will bring lower taxes but on the other hand will not ruin the budget," Cimoszewicz said.
The government proposes cutting taxes to 20, 31 and 43 percent next year from this year's 21, 33 and 45 percent.

The bigger party in the ruling coalition, the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) backs the government proposals but its smaller partner, the Polish Peasant Party (PSL) last month supported in the lower house an opposition bill introducing four levels at 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent.
The Peasants later signalled they might back out of the four-level scale if tax cuts for the low-paid were deeper than those proposed by the government.
Cimoszewicz made clear he expected President Aleksander Kwasniewski to veto the four-level scale if it cleared the Senate, a move which would effectively maintain present tax levels in 1997.

Cimoszewicz said that if the Senate passed the lower house bill and the measure was then blocked, the government would table amendments to the present tax legislation to get rid of existing loopholes.

"The government decided that if in the Senate vote a (lower house) bill on personal income taxes is unfortunately passed which would most probably not become law, we will submit a narrow tax bill amendment eliminating certain loopholes," Cimoszewicz said.
He said items that needed amendment included the current tax relief on personal donations and tax deductions on purchases of government bonds.
